newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission clears Coca-Cola buy of British bottler.
newsitem.headline: Commission clears Coca-Cola buy of British bottler.

text.p: The European Commission on Wednesday reluctantly cleared Coca-Cola Enterprises Inc to take full control of British bottler Coca-Cola & Schweppes Beverages Ltd after failing to prove the deal was a threat to competition.

Karel Van Miert, the commissioner responsible for antitrust issues in the European Union, told a news conference the deal had raised concerns at the EU competition watchdog, but that there had not been enough evidence to stop the purchase.
"We had some worries, but we have to be able to prove what might happen," Van Miert said.

Coca-Cola Enterprises, the world's largest Coke bottler, is 45 percent owned by Coca Cola Co. It has plans to acquire control of CCSB from Cadbury Schweppesthrough its purchase of Amalgamated Beverages Great Britain Ltd.
Cadbury Schweppes said the deal will give it 623 million pounds ($1 billion) to develop its branded business worldwide.

The Commission said that after an in-depth investigation of the deal it had concluded that CCSB was already dominant in the British cola market and that the deal would transfer that dominance to Coca-Cola Enterprises and Coca Cola.
But, it said, Coca Cola Co's role in CCSB was already so large that the deal would not strengthen its position under EU law.
"This dominance stems from the very high market shares of (the drink) Coca-Cola," the Commission statement said.

It noted, however, that it was investigating separately under Atricle 85 the plan for the new entity to bottle and market Cadbury Schweppes products under long-term licensing arrangements with Coca Cola Enterprises.
Van Miert said that against the views of the companies concerned, the Commission had decided that a distinct market for colas could be identifed within the soft drinks sector.
CCSB also bottles Schweppes mixers, Fanta, Sprite and Canada Dry.

The company was found to have about 60 percent of the cola market, nearly three times that of the nearest rival, Britvic, which bottles and markets Pepsi. It said a third cola, Virgin Cola, was a recent entrant and has a very small share.
The Commission said competitors had raised concerns about the potential for anti-competitive practices such as exclusivity agreements.
It overrode the concerns, however, because Article 85 would allow it to investigate accusations of malpractice at a later date if necessary.
The Commission also noted that Coca-Cola Enterprises had pledged that CCSB would not engage in such activities.
A spokesman for Coca Cola in Brussels was not immediately available for comment.
